title: Prince of Persia®: The Sands of Time
text: Pros: highly addictive. Challenging but not frustrating. Acrobatics are incredibly fun. Puzzles are interesting without stopping you dead. Fighting is tight, responsive, and gives you a fine amount of attacks, dodges and the like. Good balance of how much time you spend on the different gameplay types herein: acrobatics, dodging traps, fighting, and solving puzzles. The score is cool, rock music with a Middle Eastern touch. Likeable characters. Engaging story. The graphics hold up rather well, albeit the pre-rendered cutscenes show the limitations. Cons: some find the fighting too restrictive. The camera does get in the way, albeit using Landscape Cam, letting it "stick" to the current area for a clear view, can help. Roll and Jump are on the same key, which does mean you'll sometimes do one intending to do the other. You'll also sometimes accidentally run up a wall when you meant to run along it, and vice versa. If you play for half an hour and you don't think it's varied enough: you *will* not find the game overall to be. No collectibles, only one difficulty setting and no way for you to affect the story means little replayability. (please ignore how little time it says I've played - I've completed it several times, just not via Steam) I recommend this to any fan of fast-paced action-adventure.

title: Prince of Persia®: The Sands of Time
text: Jordan Mechner managed to do what few franchises can do: reboot the series with a game better than the original. The Sands of TIme is a masterpiece in video game design, story telling, puzzling and a somewhat functioning combat system. If you get used to the combat of dodging, wall jumping and frog jumping over enemies to defeat them, then you shouldn't have a problem, yet the combat is the weakest part of the game. It can be frustrating and you may ask yourself, "How many ♥♥♥♥ing sand soldiers are there?" as they seemingly respawn for an infinite amount during the fight sequences. What is truly remarkable about the game is the character development of the Prince and his ability to grow affectionate for a sworn enemy. Now, if you do play this game on Steam, I highly recommend using a controller and binding the keys/actions in the games options, as the Keyboard and Mouse controls are clunky and extremely frustrating where I really wanted to quit playing the game, even though I was so close to beating it. Great game, terrible PC controls, use a controller. 9.6/10

title: Prince of Persia®: The Sands of Time
text: This is my favourite POP game. I love the story, characters and level design. I'm not a big fan of third person hack&slash combat so the fact that around 50% of this game IS combat is a bit of a drawback for me but nevertheless, I still love the game overall. The game does have controller support but not in the menus. I preferred to use Xpadder to map my controls. This not only allowed me to navigate the menus with a controller but also allowed me to put a rumble on sword attacks. If you have Pinnacle or the Xpadder programs and want to play the game on your sofa through Big Picture I suggest you do the same. I played this game on Windows 10 and I've found the experience extremely frustrating at times due to a plethora of bugs. There is a bug that stops the Prince from running, a bug that makes the screen foggy so that you can't see what is happening, numerous camera angle burps that prevent the player from seeing what is going on in combat, and last but not least, an issue with the physics. Sometimes the Prince will get stuck on scenery, other times the boxes you occasionally have to push around go flying across the screen and get lodged on steps. (This last bug took me over an hour to circumnavigate using crafty bug exploits of my own) It is my belief that if a game is on sale on Steam then it should run properly on modern computer equipment. If this game was bug-free I would give it a well deserved 9/10 As it stands at the time of writing this review and in relation to the bugs I'm forced to give it a 4/10 Most of the bugs can and have been worked around by the community, and I was able to complete the game with a lot of patience. A real shame Valve doesn't hold these publishers to account. How can it be right to release buggy games to consumers? If a game is going to be placed on the Steam store front then its publishers should put forth a little effort to make sure it runs correctly.

title: Prince of Persia®: The Sands of Time
text: Even after 13 years this game still looks and plays quite well. Just be sure to turn off fog and configure your controller (double click with mouse in options menu). HOWEVER, some jumping is woefully inaccurate, the camera can be a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥sometimes, puzzles are 90% easy, but 10% of the time you wonder just where the hell you are supposed to even go. And now my biggest bug bear - combat: It would have been better to just remove it completely, because it is SO bad. You get to fight 10-20 enemies in each encounter. They respawn if you don't kill them quickly (a dagger finishing move you have to perform on every beaten enemy). They teleport after you, they swarm you and surround you, and when you're down on the floor you're as good as dead. That being said, most enemies are cannon fodder and dispatched easily enough, but some enemies (blue ones) can't be vaulted over, and they hit hard and fast, compared to the rest of the enemies. These are insanely frustrating since they make up most of the enemies encountered after the first quarter of the game. Combat is uninspired and irritating. As if that wasn't reason enough to hate it, you also have to keep an eye out on your companion, who inexplicably is NOT AT ALL able to move out of harm's way, meaning she will not move...at all, and frequently die, because she thinks she can take on a 3 meter sand monster with her bow and arrow in close combat...*sigh*. The game would be easier without her "help". Apart from that it's still an entertaining, albeit quite old, game.

title: Prince of Persia®: The Sands of Time
text: To start: I used to add a header to these reviews, but since it often made the review too long to sumbit, I've opted to leave it on my Backloggery page. Gameplay: Sid Meier has a development mantra he calls the "Covert Action Rule," which goes, "It's better to have one good game than two great games." While this isn't necessarily a perfect way to continue into this game, it's the best one I've thought of. Prince of Persia: The Sands of Time is one you probably already know about. If you don't, then what you should know is that this game is half parkour simulator and half sword-fighting game; the latter of which I found to be incredibly infuriating at times, but I'll talk about that part later. The platforming in this game is really, really fun. There's a slight bit of puzzle to the platforming sections, but usually never to the point where you've gotta stop for a minute or two to think about how you're gonna tackle these jumps. Those are saved for the actual puzzles in the game, of which there are about five puzzle areas. The first one is of the highest quality in my opinion, but that's not to say that the later ones are bad; it's just that the first one is really well-designed. As far as the controls go, there's essentially a "magic parkour button," (you should definitely use a controller for this game, by the way) and most of the actions are done automatically. This can lead you to throw yourself off of a ledge more than a few times when you're starting out, but thankfully you've got the ability to rewind time once you get the Dagger of Time. This brings me to the combat, which I feel is both far too simple and far too complex. It's far too complex, since there are apparently 50+ combos that you can do in the game, of which I only ever really needed one (attack attack attack attack etc.), and there is no documentation in-game for the combos. That's not to say that having combos are a bad thing; I'd just like to know what they are. The game does no tutorializing as far as combos go, and in fact I only learned about this vast number of combos because I looked it up. This is one of the main reasons why the game can be very frustrating; I'm assuming that these combos are in the manual or something, but the Steam version doesn't come with a manual. Even then, the combos really should be in game in a menu somewhere. Also, there were many times in which I found myself stuck on the ground and unable to get up. It turns out that if you are blocking while you're on the ground, you can't get up. The game doesn't tell you about this either. Another reason why the game is too complex for its own good is that there's only about six different types of enemies throughout the entire game, and they all pretty much have the same AI pattern of "surround player, stunlock to death," which sure does suck whenever your  only real way of getting out of that situation is jumping over enemies, and the type of enemy surrounding you are ones that can't be jumped over. The game is also far too simple, partly because of one major sin: automatic lock-on. If you are even pointing your analog stick in the directon of the enemy, you'll magically be attracted to that enemy for a while, even if you're pointing away from them. It's really annoying, and can lead to many times of getting surrounded. Trying to roll through a tight gap to avoid getting surrounded by un-jumpable enemies? Too bad; you're jumping on the un-jumpable enemy. Trying to attack a once faraway enemy that you're getting closer to? You will if you get lucky enough that the Prince stops ogling at an enemy you were attacking prior. Even beyond the frustrating bits with the controls, there's the fact that every single enemy is defeated in the same way: attack until they fall on their stomach, use the dagger to absorb them. Also yes, if you were wondering, the lock-on can mess you up with this as well, leading you to use powerups on enemies you didn't want to when you were just trying to absorb some sand. And then there's your game-long escort, Farah. Notice how I said escort and not partner? Intentional. She's an absolute idiot in combat. She comes with a bow, but constantly insists on standing statuesque directly in the fray, even when being attacked, when a much simpler solution would be for her to get to some dang high ground. There's loads of it around, so there's really no excuse for it. Also, if she dies, the game is over. What does she offer to the game as a whole? The ability to crawl through small gaps. Yes, in the grand scheme of things, she's about as useful as a puppy, mouse, or other small animal. She's about as useful in combat as well, actually. You see, she can't actually kill enemies. She just stuns them every now and then when she's not looking around in random directions admiring the architecture as though the idea of stone buildings is the most amazing thing ever. Long story short, she's absolutely useless and is more of a liablility than anything else. Speaking of the architecture (and something positive), the level design is fantastic. I'll go more into detail in the graphics section, but for now, I can definitely say that they did an excellent job creating a world that feels natural for the most part. There are a few pretty contrived places here and there, but who knows what those crazy architects are up to anymore, eh? Apart from that, though, that's all I really have to say about this game's gameplay. The platforming is super fun, but the combat just really brings the game down in my opinion. Then again, maybe games like Metal Gear Rising, Bayonetta, and Devil May Cry 1 have led me to expect too much from these kinds of games. I still stand with what I said at the beginning; this game would be so much better if it were two games: a game focused almost entirely on platforming with maybe 5% of the game being combat, and another game being 95% combat (with a more-developed combat system/enemy variety) and 5% platforming. As is, you've got one really good thing and one really frustrating thing which kinda makes me not wanna play this game again. If it weren't for the combat, this game would easily get a 10/10 from me, but with the combat, it drops to a 7/10. Great at times; absolutely miserable at others. Story: You may have gathered from that one paragraph that I don't like Farah all that much. You'd be right. To be honest, it still doesn't really make sense why she comes along at all; she's useful for being small and that's about it. All this being said though, she's not a badly written character; just an okay one. She is a love interest of the Prince, which again feels pretty contrived to me, and to be quite frank; I think the Prince is insane for wanting her. Oh well; I couldn't possibly hope to understand what goes through the Prince's head. As for the prince itself, he's pretty much straddling the line between hero and anti-hero. He wants to do good, but he's a bit of a selfish prat at the same time. Then again, he *is* a prince, so you can't expect him to have had the greatest socialization experience growing up, so fair enough. Apart from Farah and the Prince, everyone else is just a minor character. The premise and delivery is pretty cool, too; it's being told in terms of a story, and as such, has the ablility to go back and forth, as does happen with the story and the gameplay. It's all quite clever, I must admit. While the character arcs may not be the most amazing thing ever, I can appreciate the clever nature of the delivery and the premise enough to give it an 8/10. (I actually have run out of space; time to put the rest in the comments again!)

title: Prominence Poker
text: Early Access Watcher Reviews Prominence Poker Update Version: 14.320.006 Disclosure: This is a free to play game with micro-transactions, so I didn't pay for anything. Usually when you wish to find yourself at the gambling table, real money is required to buy in. Prominence Poker on the other hand provides a quick and free option to sate your poker fever. With up to six players and a booming online community, it is just a manner of downloading and jumping into a game. Unfortunately, it is never that easy when it comes to gambling simulators and the chips start to fall as soon as they are won. Prominence already wins several favor points for creating a stylized environment. Everything from the character models to the local have a solid look. Card motions such as dealing and folding are fluid while small touches such as drinking and provocation help embrace the tense mood. Background ambiance is always moving with customers walking in, interacting with items and conversing in the corner of your eye. Sound plays a similar roll with some alright music to complement the scenery. It does the required job of adding to the experience,which keeps the environment interesting enough while waiting for the AI to make their move. Poker is the name of the game and makes up the entire gameplay. There are plenty of challenges that you can complete during normal play, though I never seemed to make the challenge objectives increase no matter how many times I qualified. There is an excellent tutorial used to explain the controls. Multiplayer only supports casual games right now while single player has a practice and underground mode used sort of like a story mode. Rules are followed faithfully (from what I have seen so far), but the actual gameplay is hindered by some grim issues. It is difficult to enjoy this high stakes game when the highly annoying bugs start to set in. One such error can be extremely devastating to your progress and occurs right after a hand has been finished. The characters would simply stand or sit in a repeating loop animation while you wait for the game to reset the last hand to continue with the match. I was forced to quit the match and forfeit any chips in order to break the stale, even having to go as far as closing the client on one or two occasions. Commands can also suffer from an identity crisis as the input delay can mistake a check or raise for a fold or a call. It might have to do with the user's internet connection, but it presents a possibly dangerous issue when dealing with a fatal hand. Optimization is severely needed at a basic level to address some of the performance issues. I understand this is early access, but when it takes as much luck to draw a pair as it does to hope the game will launch without freezing, then you have a problem. Settings do not offer much in the way of customization except for a generic low to ultra graphics bar. Loading times are inherently long from starting the game to waiting for matches to load. Micro-transactions are alive and well too with their main focus revolving around cosmetics and table items that provide experience boosts. These items are bought using in-game currency, but with the inability to finish matches it becomes unlikely for one to gain them naturally. I have always been a fan of Poker and Blackjack, which is why I was so disappointed to see the issues slowing down the cards. It is very pleasing to watch with some absolutely fitting backgrounds and character models. The small details from the pedestrians playing pool to the motorcycle and laundry machine noises adding some simple ambience. Unfortunately, the cards seem to suffer from bent edges as games can suddenly lock up after hands are completed, leaving the player forced to exit the game and forfeit the chip reward. While it may not seem game breaking, the chips are crucial for online play and the attire found in the micro-transaction shop. It is with a heavy heart I give this one a pass and hope that when I review it in the future the issues are resolved. Pros - Stylized visual aesthetic - Music and sound effects breath immersion - It is Poker. Card play rules are followed strictly Cons - Micro-transactions - Game breaking issues with completed hands freezing mid game - Internet connectivity issues greatly halt game flow

title: Puzzle Dimension
text: To start at the end - Puzzle Dimension is easily the best navigation puzzle game I've ever played. Simple as that. If you look at the abundance of puzzle games created in the last ten years, you'll find plenty in all categories, if you categorize like "navigation", "construction", etc. If you categorize like "2D" and "3D" - well, you'll find hardly any in the latter category. It's not hard to see why - creating good puzzles in 3D is much tougher than in 2D, you need much more serious testing to make sure your wonderful levels don't have some silly loophole that reduces the 15-minute brain-whacking challenge to a 2-minute walkover, and since 3D puzzles are inherently more complicated than 2D puzzles, your game will be much less casual, which seriously reduces your potential audience. So from this aspect, going for a serious 3D puzzle game may look like a silly decision. And what do you call people who make such kind of silly decisions? YMMV, but I call them "heroes of the gaming industry". Doctor Entertainment took no prisoners with Puzzle Dimension. After the first few levels, it was obvious that the game was created by people with rich craftmanship in puzzle games, people who knew the rulebook well but didn't constrain themselves by it. You're guiding a ball in the game, which can roll (move 1 square), jump (move 2 squares) and later be catapulted (move 3 squares). Your objective is to collect sunflowers on levels that consist of squares, and additionally, you may want to affect (pixelate) all squares for a bonus objective. The squares can connect to each other in a single plane, but they also can connect with 45-degree deviation, which means after two steps you're perpendicular to your previous position, and after four steps you're upside down. The gravity is always related to the square you're on, so you won't fall - but you can jump / roll off, and if there's no square under you, you're dead. This set of rules enables the creatiion of horrenduously complicated levels, and later in the game, there'll be some. Puzzles start out in a gentle manner, but starting from level 4 or 5, they're not quite obvious. New mechanics are introduced about every five levels - you generally have one simple level to experiment with your new block type, and then there are four more medium headscratchers. That goes on until level 50 (or the first five clusters), then you have two thematic clusters - #6 is called Bends, which showcases the 3D connection method I outlined in the previous paragraph, and gives a teaser of what will come in the last two clusters. Then #8 (revisited) is a kind of remix of earlier levels, big, sprawling and hugely enjoyable puzzles. Non-hardcore puzzle players should consider to stop here... ... because the last two clusters feel more like tactical warfare than a puzzle game. As the conclusion of the game, you get 20 puzzles you need to explore thoroughly, and think about your completion strategy, as you might paint yourself in a corner with your first step already. These levels took quite serious time and effort, but the level of satisfaction gained is massively superior to almost any other game I played. There's no navigation puzzle game that ever came close, and in the entire puzzle "universe", only SpaceChem was better. When I completed the last level (after forty-odd minutes of wrestling with a level that felt like a bona fide roguelike game), it did feel like a huge victory. Presentation is also worth a few words. The game looks pretty enough with the initial pixelated look, but when you affect the squares, they turn into very nice hi-res blocks. There are four visual themes available (they unlock as you progress), and all of them are beautiful. Sound design is also excellent, with the ball clattering on standard blocks, scraping on ice, or the catapult (spring) blocks making huge noise when launching the ball. The music rounds out the experience nicely. All in all, it's not too tall to say that Puzzle Dimension is as perfect a navigation puzzle game as it's possible to come close to perfection. I spent more than 15 hours solving its puzzles, and that contained no silly cutscenes and no time wasting. This game stands head and shoulders above the other entrants in its category - if you're looking for a brainy challenge on the PC, this game will surely deliver. Most recommended.

title: Puzzle Dimension
text: You like gentle-paced 3D visual/spatial puzzlers. Kula World anyone? A very unassuming, yet enjoyable marble-rolling 3D puzzler. I tend to forget it's there, then go back to it and go "oh hey, I forgot this was pretty neat!" - You basically roll around the level with the aim to collect all of the sunflowers to unlock the exit. Why a ball need sunflowers is anybody's guess... But screw it, it looks nice. The challenge, of course, is in the myriad of tiles introduced along the way. Some collapse after you have used them once, others have spikes that can be deactivated with a switch... and the classic: Ice which keeps you rolling in the same direction - often off the edge of the board. But this is only half the challenge. When rolling over curved blocks, your orientation and gravity shift with it too, adding a neat dynamic to the game. Sometimes the only way to reach a certain spot above you is to roll around so that it ends up below you, allowing gravity to do its thing. Add into this the regular additions of new blocks, and this makes for a decent puzzler that picks up difficulty pretty nicely - many levels often needing a few attempts to fully crack. I'm not even halfway, so estimate you should be able to get at least a good 10 hours out of this one. Not bad at all for a puzzler. It looks nice but could perhaps be a bit 'cleaner' / more zen (akin to the likes of Quell, Patterna and Hexcells). Right now it feels like it's not sure what its design should be... particularly in combining HD and retro into some sort of arcade machine. I'm not a big fan of the retro music and sounds, which leaves it feeling a little jarring. That said, the pixelated blocks changing into beautiful HD as you roll near them is an interesting touch and makes for a nice extra to 'paint' the whole level so to speak. So it's a bit slow to get into and not as engrossing as other head-scratchers out there. But the puzzles are plenty and well-crafted enough to give you something to sink your teeth into. Overall, I'd say it's a well-balanced mix of trial-and-error with sufficient "oh! I think I've spotted how to do it!" to keep it rewarding. The metallic ball does not contain an infinity stone. I've tried looking.

text: This game pushes further into alternative gameplay systems than Transistor did. It's a very distinct departure from both Bastion and Transistor that still retains the spirit of those two games while providing a unique and creative core gameplay loop. A big chunk of the gameplay is spent performing 'rites,' which are basically rituals that play a little bit like a game of basketball or something. You summon 3 members of your party into a rite and can only control one of them at a time. Each party member has their own abilities, advantages, and disadvantages. The rest of the gameplay is boils down to dialogue choices that can provide items or modify the stats of some characters for upcoming rites. The writing and characters of this game are the meat, though. You'll find a cast of lovable characters playing out a story set in a magical world brought to life by Supergiant's fantastic visuals and music. Everything about this game's presentation is fantastic and the people at Supergiant have outdone themselves in this regard for the 2nd time in a row. While I don't think the gameplay on offer here will please everyone as much as Bastion's or Transistor's did, I really enjoyed it and I think it's worth experiencing the game just to watch the story unfold. Once again, Supergiant Games has reminded me why I love video games.

title: Pyre
text: That is a hyperbole, of course. Yet rarely if ever have I played a game that was such a complete package whilst exceeding in nearly every category and failing in no perceivable aspect. I have heaped praise upon Supergiant Games' works before, but I fully believe that Pyre stands head and shoulders above Bastion and Transistor. If you wish for a more measured review, look elsewhere. I have loved the game and urge you with all my heart for you to play it. This review will instead focus more on comparing Pyre to its two predecessors, and see how I feel it measures up. The reason I took so long to play Pyre is because I truly believed I would dislike its gameplay. It is a sports game - after a fashion - and that isn't something I appreciate. My fears were soon quenched, however, as Pyre's gameplay proved itself a stupidly fast-paced, diverse and engaging experience, all the while containing the action to a single small field, six players and a ball. It is a condensation of everything that made Bastion and Transistor stand out, a microcosm that packs an unbelievable punch. Every match is different than the last. The terrain, environmental effects, each one of the six players on the field, their skills and items - any alteration in any of those variables can make for an entirely unique experience. If you are intimidated by Pyre's gameplay being like a sports game - fear not. You will be white-knuckled in excitement in no time. The rest of Pyre's gameplay consists of an Oregon Trail-ish roaming about the magnificent environs, choosing which paths to take, not unlike Banner Saga. Orienting yourself by the stars is a nice touch that melds world-building into decision-making. I am not knowledgeable about music - at all. So take everything I say here with a grain of salt. Pyre's music is on par with its predecessors - though I do believe it takes a definitive edge by the way in which it is used. The vocals always kick in to throw the dramatic curve over the edge, to outline the stakes of everything you're doing. And, best of all, they subtly alter their lines in accordance to who you're fighting, and the final outcome of the game. Nothing as iconic or immediatelly quotable as Build that Wall from Bastion - yet still, I feel, more impactful. As wonderful and engaging as Caelondia or Cloudbank. Perhaps more. I feel the world is much more fleshed out, but that isn't really the point. Pyre's narrative - is one that you, the player, build yourself, through the Rites you perform, through the characters you choose, and- through both victory and defeat. Pyre has no apparent explicit or implied fail state, insofar as story progression is concerned. There are no possible Game Overs. Whether you succeed or fail, the story continues, taking that failure into account. Experience is awarded to your character regardless of the outcome of the match. The point of the Rites isn't victory - but Enlightenment. Every one of those twists and turns can affect the ending, leading to an embarassingly large number of them - for they revolve around the fates of each particular character, and their contributions to the state of things after the game is over. There is no Best Ending, or True Ending. This is what makes Pyre even more heartwrenching than its predecessors. There are instead a multitude of endings, none of which can satisfy the existential void which sets in. This pain - it is a bittersweet pain. Pyre -is- its characters. And this is the crucial point. Supergiant Games excel in most aspects, but I feel like Bastion and Transistor's characters weren't the focus of their respective games. To be sure, there are good characters in those games- -But they cannot hope to compare to Pyre. Pyre has a stable of characters with both variety and depth. Companions and rivals. Playable and non-playable. It feels like each character is important in and of itself, as you discover more about them, as you have repeated exchanges with them, friendly or otherwise, growing closer and more familiar. And it is, of course, reinforced by gameplay. Each playable character plays differently, as does every rival character. And you have a real stake in deciding what happens to each one of them, and how these decisions will organically weave new threads between them and throughout the major story. And what happens to each and every one of them is both a source of joy and sadness alike, especially because you know you had a hand in their fates. You might even feel tempted to purposefully lose a match or two, in order to ensure a brighter future for one of your favorite rivals. All of this in turn leads back to the sheer variety of endings. Pyre's greatest strength is the way gameplay, narrative, characters and even music are tightly bound together into a complete, amazing package. What are you doing? Play it already!

text: It was a good story-driven game.  You'll actually give something of a rat's♥♥♥♥♥about your companions, and the game presents you with many difficult choices regarding whether to help them, even if it hurts yourself or the team.  It's like the 9 musketeers, all for one, except when it's one for all. The actual sports-ball game is pretty good - it's sufficiently challenging on the medium difficulty level, and you can always increase the difficulty or use modifiers to up the challenge (and reward you with more XP).  Most characters play very differently from the others, and the perks you can unlock with them as they gain XP enhance their niche roles.  It's very satisfying to figure out which characters complement others in unique ways, and scoring a point is rewarding. The sound is superb, with custom music that is sad, adventurous, or compelling where appropriate.  The narrator character is awesome - he sounds like Alan Rickman and is equal parts insulting and begrudgingly respectful - he'll taunt you when you teamwipe or blunder, and congratulate you when you score. All in all well worth playing.  I'll give it another go-through someday on a harder difficulty level next time and see what happens!

title: Pyre
text: TL;DR: A good game from Supergiant Games, definitely recommend playing it. But beware, there is much to read and if you don't like the core gameplay (the rites) then this game will disappoint you. Gorgeous and breathtaking art aside, this games core mechanic, the Rites, is a really fun kind of soccer, almost reminiscent of Mario Strikers: Charged, but also vastly different in style. The different characters have different abilities with weaknesses and strengths, making it crucial to choose the right team against the opponents you are facing. Main goal is to push a ball in the enemies fire (the pyre) and extinguish it, either by tossing yourself with the ball in there (easier, but with drawbacks for the next round) or just tossing the ball (more difficult, because easily interruptable, but no drawbacks). The enemy however, having the same abilities as you, won't make it easy on you and every Rite plays different. There is more, the story is also quite intriguing, slowly opening up to the player as he goes his way. The characters all have their own quirks and almost all of them are likable in their own way. However, the game gains another component after aprox. 4 hours of playtime, opening it up more, but also falling into repetition gameplay-wise. Midgame you experience the same procedure again and again, always interrupted by different story bits, but still, it is a loop and the story does not really move at this point. Unfortunately I am quite sure the many "choices" you can make throughout the game (don't want to spoil anything) will not amount to as many endings as it wnats you to believe, because the sheer number of possible outcomes cannot be programmed into this little game. All in all, the beautiful art, the unique gameplay and the possibilities unfolding as I play make this game pretty good. This certainly gets a high recommendation, everyone should try this, but also beware, there is much text and a lot of repeting gameplay mechanics midgame, making it a game that is NOT for everyone. Not Supergiants best game, especially story-wise, but very enjoyable nonetheless (for me at least).

title: Q.U.B.E: Director's Cut
text: QUBE proves that even if you have no design ability, no artistic skill, no programming ability, and no creativity whatsoever, you can still make a video game.  The basic gameplay loop is that you enter a white room, look for the three or four colored blocks, click on them in the correct order, and then move on to the next room.  It's basically a paint by numbers puzzle game where someone forgot to paint the numbers. Aside from the utter lack of anything resembling artwork in the game, the puzzles themselves are pretty boring and pointless.  The block elements in the game don't really lend themselves to interesting or intuitive puzzles, and your interactions with the various blocks are limited to one of two actions. Also, in the director's cut, there's some sort of thin, pointless story thrown on top.  It's totally disconnected from the game however, so instead of being mildly annoying like most pointless stories in video games, in QUBE it's actively distracting since you'll be scratching your head trying to figure out what the story has to do with the boring white room you're currently in.

title: Q.U.B.E: Director's Cut
text: When I think of every puzzle game I've played on Steam recently, I realize that this game, unlike them, can't boast anything unique or innovative. The main puzzle elements and gimmicks are not remotely new. The plot is a retread of ground over which we've already built a four-lane highway, you know exactly how it's going to play out literally the second you hear the second person talk. Atmosphere is desperately trying to rip off Portal 1 and 2, minus the dialog, and mostly without success. In a few places (ie the parts with blue blocks at the bottom of ramps) it's so blatant it's distracting. Pacing is also bad; there's many parts where you have to wait on slow elevators for no reason. The puzzles are good I geuss, or at least some of the ones near the end are good and the progression of how it introduces new stuff is handled well. But the game's also terribly short. Steam says I only played for 2 hours and I beat the story and 2 hidden bonus puzzles, and since there's no medals, collectibles or rankings in the main game (outside the DLC racing side-levels) it has 0 replayability. I've described games as "short" which were more than twice this long and had better reasons to revisit the levels to boot. Oh, and in the lasers+mirrors puzzles they literally didn't program in mirror behavior for anything but the correct solutions, which is baffling. Pretty much the only thing it has going for it is the graphics, which are great for an indie game. Otherwise, I wouldn't recommend this.

title: Q.U.B.E: Director's Cut
text: Q.U.B.E. - Quality... Underrated... Brain.... Enjoyment? ¯\_(ツ)_/¯ ----- You wouldn't be alone in looking at the marketing for this game and thinking it looks like a knock-off Portal. The truth is that's more or less correct, but Q.U.B.E. is just unique enough and the idea itself is good enough for that to not really matter. The game's puzzles were, I thought, actually kind of exciting. They rely more on straightforward logic than trial and error and finding the solutions was quite satisfying. The narrative which accompanies them was also quite strong (due in large part to some excellent voice acting), though somewhat farfetched. If you can put your sense of disbelief to one side, it's an enjoyable, more-serious-than-portal-whilst-nodding-at-it-in-passing yarn. Overall, it's short and sweet. If you can get it for cheap and like a puzzle game then I definitely recommend spending a couple hours with it.

text: Q.U.B.E: Directors Cut is a short and fun puzzle game (That wouldn`t exist without portal). You play as a man without his memory (Thanks Portal). You wear a glove and control qubes in the environment. There are five type of qubes. Red qubes, yellow cubes, green qubes, blue qubes and purple qubes. Each qubes works differently. Blue qubes qorks like a spring board while yellow qubes act as steps. There are a few twists and turnes in regards to the puzzle mechanins, but that is the general mechanins. The most disapointing thing about this game to me was the final level. It didn`t combine all the mechanincs learned like Portal, instead it just used a new set. It was still a fun game that only lasted about 3 hours.

title: Q.U.B.E: Director's Cut
text: Portal comparisons must be made: It is a series of puzzle based rooms that may or may not be test chambers all from the first person perspective as a mystery is slowly unravelled as you go. Portal portal PORTAL! Besides the obvious comparison this is not a bad little game. In Q.U.B.E. you have a pair of magical-science gloves that can manipulate a series of coloured cubes with various different properties e.g. red cubes just extend out as platforms, yellow cubes a series of three platforms, blue launching anything that touches it etc... While this may sound greatly varied they are, for better or worse, mostly just variants on platforms. As the game progresses more interesting items appear such as coloured balls that need depositing in pits, rotating rooms, rooms with lightswitches (more interesting then it sounds) and the ability to change cubes to whatever colour you choose. Despite all these fun sounding mechanics, the game is visually a very sterile white consistently. While Portal was mostly sterile, there were moments where you had variations in the chamber and moments where you could go behind the chambers, in Q.U.B.E. it remains almost exclusively cold white rooms. Late in the game things break up a little , but not to a great extent. The Director's Cut version adds both a narration via two characters talking to you via a radio, never fully being seen in game, and also changes some of the chambers layouts around. The naration helps to a degree as, with the first version, I found myself getting bored of the repetative rooms with no context. While it can be seen as a boon, it almost instantly breaks the late game twists by telling you right away what is going on, though it does provide a nice conflict for the player that is only answered at the end of the game. A recommendation for a rainy day as (I'M MENTIONING PORTAL AGAIN) with the first Portal game it is very short. Grab it when on offer or when it hits an indie bundle.

Which also kills the moral of the story, sadly. -No subtitles Pros: -Story It was a great set up, till the end. -Music Amazing soundtrack fits the tone and situation well. nothing memoriable in my book, but still it's has an exceptional ost -Atmostphere It is both an awesome and cryptic place, you have no idea where you are, and where you are heading. This is the strongest comparison to portal. -Variety Lot of great mechanics. I can't see how you'd get bored. -Tutorial It feeds you info by level design. THERE IS NO HAND HOLDING IN THIS GAME! Makes it a lot easier to replay. Conclusion: Qube is okay. I don't regret buying, or playing it. I'm just sad there was all lot of wasted potiental.
